df7dddc6-a4fd-5b1b-9b73-8528e5224ca9.title: Integrating a Reciprocal Function and Simplifying the Arbitrary Constant Using the Laws of Logarithms

e-374.worked_solution:
First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $2$ out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of $\dfrac 1 x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{2}{x})\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2ln⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

e-375.knowledge_point: Integrating the Sum of a Reciprocal Function and a Power Function
e-375.problem: Find the integral of $\dfrac 1 {2x} + 3x$ with respect to $x.$
e-375.worked_solution:
Applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{1}{2x}+3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2x}\,\text{d}x+\int 3x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+3\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}ln⁡|x|+3\cdot \frac{{x}^{1+1}}{1+1}+C \\  & =\frac{ln⁡|x|}{2}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

e-376.knowledge_point: Integrating a Reciprocal Function and Simplifying the Arbitrary Constant Using the Laws of Logarithms
e-376.worked_solution:
We separate the integrand into the sum of two fractions so that we can simplify each term. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3+2x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{3}{x}+\frac{2x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{3}{x}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+2\int \,\text{d}x \\  & =3ln⁡|x|+2x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C =3 \ln K$ where $K$ is some other constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $3\ln|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3+2x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =3ln⁡|x|+2x+C \\  & =3ln⁡|x|+2x+3ln⁡K \\  & =3ln⁡(K|x|)+2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate ∫−3xdx=

a
3ln⁡x+C
b
−3ln⁡|x|+C
c
3ln⁡|x|+C
d
−3ln⁡|x|+C

decision.explanation: Take the constant −3 outside the integral. Since ∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| + C, the result is −3ln|x| + C.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $-3$ out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of $\frac{1}{x},$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{3}{x}\,\text{d}x & =-3\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3ln⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3

Calculate ∫10xdx.

a
10ln⁡|x|+C
b
10+ln⁡|x|+C
c
ln⁡|x|+C
d
ln⁡|x|10+C

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $10$ out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of $\frac{1}{x},$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{10}{x}\,\text{d}x & =10\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =10ln⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 4
?

Calculate ∫−17xdx.

a
−17ln⁡|x|+C
b
−7ln⁡|x|+C
c
−77ln⁡|x|+C
d
−ln⁡|7x|+C
e
−77ln⁡|x|+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Factor out −1/√7 and integrate 1/x to obtain −(1/√7)ln|x| + C. Rationalizing gives −(√7/7)ln|x| + C.

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{7}}=-\frac{\sqrt{7}}{7}$ out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of $\frac{1}{x},$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{7}}{7}ln⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient −17=−1777=−77 out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of 1x, and get ∫−17xdx=−17∫1xdx=−77ln⁡|x|+C.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms that factoring out −1/√7 and using ∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| + C gives −(√7/7)ln|x| + C, option c.

content.worked_solution:
First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{7}}=-\frac{\sqrt{7}}{7}$ out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of $\frac{1}{x},$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{7}}{7}ln⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: For x > 0, √(x³)/√(x⁵) = x^(3/2−5/2) = 1/x. Thus the integrand is −4/x, whose integral is −4ln|x| + C.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Find the integral of $\frac{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}{\sqrt{{x}^{5}}}-5{x}^{-1}$ with respect to $x.$
after.worked_solution:
Simplifying the exponents and applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}{\sqrt{{x}^{5}}}-5{x}^{-1})\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{5/2-3/2}}\,\text{d}x-5\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x-5\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4ln⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}

Question 6
?

Find the integral of x3x5−5x−1 with respect to x.

a
4ln⁡|x|+C
b
−4ln⁡|x|+C
c
−5ln⁡|x|+C
d
−6x+C
e
5x+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Simplifying the exponents and applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

∫(x3x5−5x−1)dx=∫1x5/2−3/2dx−5∫1xdx=∫1xdx−5∫1xdx=−4∫1xdx=−4ln⁡|x|+C.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms that the radical quotient simplifies to 1/x. Combining terms gives −4/x, whose integral is −4ln|x| + C.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating the Sum of a Reciprocal Function and a Power Function
content.problem: Find the integral of $\frac{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}{\sqrt{{x}^{5}}}-5{x}^{-1}$ with respect to $x.$
content.worked_solution:
Simplifying the exponents and applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}{\sqrt{{x}^{5}}}-5{x}^{-1})\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{5/2-3/2}}\,\text{d}x-5\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x-5\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4ln⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: Find the integral of ${(2-\frac{1}{x})}^{2}$ with respect to $x.$
after.worked_solution:
Expanding the binomial and applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(2-\frac{1}{x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =\int (4-\frac{4}{x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})\text{d}x \\  & =\int 4\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{4}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\int \text{d}x-4\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4x-4ln⁡|x|+\frac{{x}^{-2+1}}{-2+1}+C \\  & =4x-4ln⁡|x|-\frac{1}{x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 9
?

Find the integral of 3x−1+3x−1 with respect to x.

a
32x2+3ln⁡|x|+C
b
12x2+3ln⁡|x|+C
c
52x2+4ln⁡|x|+C
d
23x2+2ln⁡|x|+C
e
43x2+5ln⁡|x|+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Since 3/x⁻¹ = 3x, the integrand is 3x + 3/x. Integrating term by term gives (3/2)x² + 3ln|x| + C.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Find the integral of $\frac{3}{{x}^{-1}}+3{x}^{-1}$ with respect to $x.$
after.worked_solution:
Applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{3}{{x}^{-1}}+3{x}^{-1})\text{d}x & =3\int x\,\text{d}x+3\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+3ln⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Find the integral of 3x−1+3x−1 with respect to x.

a
32x2+3ln⁡|x|+C
b
12x2+3ln⁡|x|+C
c
52x2+4ln⁡|x|+C
d
23x2+2ln⁡|x|+C
e
43x2+5ln⁡|x|+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

∫(3x−1+3x−1)dx=3∫xdx+3∫1xdx=32x2+3ln⁡|x|+C.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating the Sum of a Reciprocal Function and a Power Function
content.problem: Find the integral of $\frac{3}{{x}^{-1}}+3{x}^{-1}$ with respect to $x.$
content.worked_solution:
Applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{3}{{x}^{-1}}+3{x}^{-1})\text{d}x & =3\int x\,\text{d}x+3\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+3ln⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Apply the power rule: ∫2x^(7/3) dx = (3/5)x^(10/3). Also, ∫−1/(3x) dx = −(1/3)ln|x|. Adding gives option b.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Find the integral of $2{x}^{7/3}-\frac{1}{3x}$ with respect to $x.$
after.worked_solution:
Applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (2{x}^{7/3}-\frac{1}{3x})\text{d}x & =\int 2{x}^{7/3}\,\text{d}x-\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{x}^{7/3+1}}{(\frac{7}{3}+1)}-\frac{1}{3}ln⁡|x|+C \\  & =\frac{3}{5}{x}^{10/3}-\frac{1}{3}ln⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 11
?

What is the antiderivative of (1+1x)2?

a
1−1x+2ln⁡(|K|x)
b
x−1x+2ln⁡(K|x|)
c
1+2ln⁡(|K|x)
d
x+(1+ln⁡(K|x|))2
e
x−1x+ln⁡(2K|x|)
Submit

decision.explanation: Expand to 1+2/x+1/x² and integrate to get x−1/x+2ln|x|+C. Writing C=2ln K, with K>0, combines the logarithms into 2ln(K|x|), giving option b.

after.name: Question 11
after.worked_solution:
Expanding the binomial and applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(1+\frac{1}{x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =\int (1+\frac{2}{x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x+2\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x+2ln⁡|x|+\frac{{x}^{-2+1}}{-2+1}+C \\  & =x+2ln⁡|x|-\frac{1}{x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=2ln⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $2ln⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(1+\frac{1}{x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =x-\frac{1}{x}+2ln⁡|x|+2ln⁡K \\  & =x-\frac{1}{x}+2(ln⁡|x|+ln⁡K) \\  & =x-\frac{1}{x}+2ln⁡(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

What is the antiderivative of (1+1x)2?

a
1−1x+2ln⁡(|K|x)
b
x−1x+2ln⁡(K|x|)
c
1+2ln⁡(|K|x)
d
x+(1+ln⁡(K|x|))2
e
x−1x+ln⁡(2K|x|)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Expanding the binomial and applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

∫(1+1x)2dx=∫(1+2x+1x2)dx=∫dx+2∫1xdx+∫1x2dx=x+2ln⁡|x|+x−2+1−2+1+C=x+2ln⁡|x|−1x+C.

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant C, we can always write C=2ln⁡K where K is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with 2ln⁡|x| term, and we get

∫(1+1x)2dx=x−1x+2ln⁡|x|+2ln⁡K=x−1x+2(ln⁡|x|+ln⁡K)=x−1x+2ln⁡(K|x|).

content.worked_solution:
Expanding the binomial and applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(1+\frac{1}{x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =\int (1+\frac{2}{x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x+2\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x+2ln⁡|x|+\frac{{x}^{-2+1}}{-2+1}+C \\  & =x+2ln⁡|x|-\frac{1}{x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=2ln⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $2ln⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(1+\frac{1}{x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =x-\frac{1}{x}+2ln⁡|x|+2ln⁡K \\  & =x-\frac{1}{x}+2(ln⁡|x|+ln⁡K) \\  & =x-\frac{1}{x}+2ln⁡(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Expand to 1+3/x+9/(4x²). Integrating gives x−9/(4x)+3ln|x|+C. Writing C=3ln K for K>0 gives x−9/(4x)+3ln(K|x|), option c.

after.name: Question 12
after.worked_solution:
Expanding the binomial and applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(1+\frac{3}{2x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =\int (1+\frac{3}{x}+\frac{9}{4{x}^{2}})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x+3\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\frac{9}{4}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x+3ln⁡|x|+\frac{9{x}^{-2+1}}{4(-2+1)}+C \\  & =x+3ln⁡|x|-\frac{9}{4x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=3ln⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $3ln⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(1+\frac{3}{2x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =x-\frac{9}{4x}+3ln⁡|x|+3ln⁡K \\  & =x-\frac{9}{4x}+3(ln⁡|x|+ln⁡K) \\  & =x-\frac{9}{4x}+3ln⁡(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=3ln⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $3ln⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(1+\frac{3}{2x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =x-\frac{9}{4x}+3ln⁡|x|+3ln⁡K \\  & =x-\frac{9}{4x}+3(ln⁡|x|+ln⁡K) \\  & =x-\frac{9}{4x}+3ln⁡(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $2$ out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of $\frac{1}{x},$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2{x}^{-1}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2ln⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=2ln⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $2ln⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2{x}^{-1}\,\text{d}x & =2ln⁡|x|+2ln⁡K \\  & =2(ln⁡|x|+ln⁡K) \\  & =2ln⁡(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13

What is the antiderivative of 2x−1?

a
2ln⁡(K|x|)
b
ln⁡(K|x|)2
c
2ln⁡(K|x|)
d
ln⁡(K|x|2)
e
ln⁡(2K|x|)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient 2 out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of 1x, and get

∫2x−1dx=2∫1xdx=2ln⁡|x|+C.

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant C, we can always write C=2ln⁡K where K is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with 2ln⁡|x| term, and we get

∫2x−1dx=2ln⁡|x|+2ln⁡K=2(ln⁡|x|+ln⁡K)=2ln⁡(K|x|).

$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=2ln⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $2ln⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2{x}^{-1}\,\text{d}x & =2ln⁡|x|+2ln⁡K \\  & =2(ln⁡|x|+ln⁡K) \\  & =2ln⁡(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 14
after.worked_solution:
First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $-\frac{5}{2}$ out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of $\frac{1}{x},$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{5}{2x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{5}{2}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}ln⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=-\frac{5}{2}ln⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $-\frac{5}{2}ln⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{5}{2x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{5}{2}ln⁡|x|-\frac{5}{2}ln⁡K \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}(ln⁡|x|+ln⁡K) \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}ln⁡(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14

What is the antiderivative of −52x?

a
−52ln⁡(|x|+K)
b
−ln⁡(52K|x|)
c
52ln⁡(K|x|)
d
−52ln⁡(K|x|)
e
12ln⁡(5K|x|)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient −52 out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of 1x, and get

∫−52xdx=−52∫1xdx=−52ln⁡|x|+C.

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant C, we can always write C=−52ln⁡K where K is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with −52ln⁡|x| term, and we get

∫−52xdx=−52ln⁡|x|−52ln⁡K=−52(ln⁡|x|+ln⁡K)=−52ln⁡(K|x|).

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms −(5/2)ln|x|+C. Writing C=−(5/2)ln K for K>0 gives −(5/2)ln(K|x|), option d. Its derivative is −5/(2x).

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Reciprocal Function and Simplifying the Arbitrary Constant Using the Laws of Logarithms
content.worked_solution:
First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $-\frac{5}{2}$ out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of $\frac{1}{x},$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{5}{2x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{5}{2}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}ln⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=-\frac{5}{2}ln⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $-\frac{5}{2}ln⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{5}{2x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{5}{2}ln⁡|x|-\frac{5}{2}ln⁡K \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}(ln⁡|x|+ln⁡K) \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}ln⁡(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Integrating 5/(2x) gives (5/2)ln|x|+C. Writing C=(5/2)ln K with K>0 gives (5/2)ln(K|x|), option c.

after.name: Question 15
after.worked_solution:
First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $\frac{5}{2}$ out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of $\frac{1}{x},$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{2x}\text{d}x & =\frac{5}{2}\int \frac{1}{x}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}ln⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=\frac{5}{2}ln⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $\frac{5}{2}ln⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{2x}\text{d}x & =\frac{5}{2}ln⁡|x|+\frac{5}{2}ln⁡K \\  & =\frac{5}{2}(ln⁡|x|+ln⁡K) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}ln⁡(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient 52 out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of 1x, and get

∫52xdx=52∫1xdx=52ln⁡|x|+C.

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant C, we can always write C=52ln⁡K where K is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with 52ln⁡|x| term, and we get

∫52xdx=52ln⁡|x|+52ln⁡K=52(ln⁡|x|+ln⁡K)=52ln⁡(K|x|).

First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $\frac{5}{2}$ out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of $\frac{1}{x},$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{2x}\text{d}x & =\frac{5}{2}\int \frac{1}{x}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}ln⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=\frac{5}{2}ln⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $\frac{5}{2}ln⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{2x}\text{d}x & =\frac{5}{2}ln⁡|x|+\frac{5}{2}ln⁡K \\  & =\frac{5}{2}(ln⁡|x|+ln⁡K) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}ln⁡(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$
